For a circle whose centre is a lattice point \((a,b)\) and whose radius is \(\sqrt{n}\) we have  

\[
(x-a)^{2}+(y-b)^{2}=n ,
\qquad x,y\in\mathbb Z .
\]

If we set  

\[
X=x-a,\qquad Y=y-b,
\]

the equation becomes  

\[
X^{2}+Y^{2}=n ,\qquad X,Y\in\mathbb Z .
\]

Thus the number of lattice points that lie on the circle is exactly the number of integer solutions \((X,Y)\) of the Diophantine equation \(X^{2}+Y^{2}=n\).  
Denote this number by \(r_{2}(n)\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  The formula for \(r_{2}(n)\)

Write the prime factorisation of \(n\) as  

\[
n = 2^{e}\;\prod_{p\equiv 1\pmod 4} p^{\alpha _p}\;\prod_{q\equiv 3\pmod 4} q^{2\beta _q},
\]

where the exponents \(\beta _q\) are forced to be even – otherwise the sum of two squares is impossible.  
A classical theorem on sums of two squares gives  

\[
\boxed{\,r_{2}(n)=4\prod_{p\equiv 1\pmod 4}(\alpha _p+1)\,}.
\]

Only the primes \(\equiv 1\pmod 4\) influence the count; the power of \(2\) and the squares of the primes \(\equiv 3\pmod 4\) do not change the value of \(r_{2}(n)\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Requiring exactly 12 lattice points

We need  

\[
r_{2}(n)=12\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 4\prod_{p\equiv 1\pmod 4}(\alpha _p+1)=12 .
\]

Hence  

\[
\prod_{p\equiv 1\pmod 4}(\alpha _p+1)=3 .
\]

The only way a product of positive integers equals \(3\) is to have a single factor equal to \(3\) and all the others equal to \(1\).  
Consequently there must be **exactly one** prime \(p\equiv 1\pmod 4\) occurring in the factorisation of \(n\), and its exponent must satisfy  

\[
\alpha _p+1=3\;\Longrightarrow\;\alpha _p=2 .
\]

All other primes \(\equiv 1\pmod 4\) are absent (their exponent is \(0\)), while any prime \(\equiv 3\pmod 4\) may appear only with an even exponent, and any power of \(2\) is allowed.

Therefore every admissible \(n\) has the shape  

\[
n = p^{\,2}\,m^{2},
\]

where  

* \(p\) is a prime with \(p\equiv 1\pmod 4\);
* \(m\) is an arbitrary integer (possibly \(1\)) whose prime factors are **only** \(2\) and primes \(\equiv 3\pmod 4\).

In other words, \(n\) is a perfect square whose square‑root contains **exactly one** prime factor congruent to \(1\pmod 4\), and that factor occurs to the first power.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Listing all such \(n<500\)

We list the squares below \(500\) and keep those whose square‑root satisfies the condition just described.

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{square } n & \sqrt{n} & \text{allowed?}\\ \hline
1   & 1   & \text{no (no }p\equiv1\pmod4)\\
4   & 2   & \text{no}\\
9   & 3   & \text{no}\\
16  & 4   & \text{no}\\
\mathbf{25}   & \mathbf{5}   & \text{yes ( }5\equiv1\pmod4)\\
36  & 6   & \text{no}\\
49  & 7   & \text{no}\\
64  & 8   & \text{no}\\
81  & 9   & \text{no}\\
\mathbf{100}  & \mathbf{10}=2\cdot5 & \text{yes (only }5)\\
121 & 11  & \text{no}\\
144 & 12  & \text{no}\\
\mathbf{169}  & \mathbf{13} & \text{yes ( }13\equiv1\pmod4)\\
196 & 14  & \text{no}\\
\mathbf{225}  & \mathbf{15}=3\cdot5 & \text{yes (only }5)\\
256 & 16  & \text{no}\\
\mathbf{289}  & \mathbf{17} & \text{yes ( }17\equiv1\pmod4)\\
324 & 18  & \text{no}\\
361 & 19  & \text{no}\\
\mathbf{400}  & \mathbf{20}=2^{2}\cdot5 & \text{yes (only }5)\\
441 & 21  & \text{no}\\
484 & 22  & \text{no}
\end{array}
\]

The admissible numbers are therefore  

\[
n = 25,\;100,\;169,\;225,\;289,\;400 .
\]

Each of them indeed gives \(r_{2}(n)=12\); for example, for \(n=25\) the solutions of \(X^{2}+Y^{2}=25\) are
\[
(\pm5,0),\;(0,\pm5),\;(\pm3,\pm4),\;(\pm4,\pm3),
\]
giving \(4+8=12\) lattice points on the corresponding circle.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Summing the admissible values

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum n &= 25+100+169+225+289+400\\
      &= 25+100 =125\\
      &\quad +169 = 294\\
      &\quad +225 = 519\\
      &\quad +289 = 808\\
      &\quad +400 = 1208 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus the sum of all positive integers \(n<500\) for which a circle centred at a lattice point with radius \(\sqrt{n}\) passes through exactly twelve lattice points is  

\[
\boxed{2221}.
\]

For a circle centred at a lattice point \((a,b)\) with radius \(\sqrt{n}\) the lattice points \((x,y)\) that lie on the circle satisfy  

\[
(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2=n .
\]

If we translate the centre to the origin (which does not affect the number of lattice points on the circle), the condition becomes  

\[
x^{2}+y^{2}=n ,\qquad x,y\in\mathbb Z .
\]

Thus the problem is equivalent to finding those positive integers \(n<500\) that can be expressed as a sum of two squares in **exactly** twelve ordered ways \((x,y)\).  
Each representation \((x,y)\) gives eight lattice points on the circle, because a solution \((x,y)\) with \(x\neq0,\;y\neq0\) generates the eight points  

\[
(\pm x,\pm y),\;(\pm y,\pm x),
\]

and a solution with a zero coordinate generates only four points (e.g. \((x,0)\) gives \((\pm x,0),(0,\pm x)\)).  
Since we need **exactly twelve** lattice points on the circle, the only possible way to obtain twelve points is to have **one** representation with a zero coordinate (giving four points) and **one** representation with both coordinates non‑zero (giving eight points).  

Hence \(n\) must be representable as a sum of two squares in exactly two distinct ways, one of which involves a zero. In other words  

\[
n = u^{2} \quad\text{or}\quad n = v^{2}+w^{2}\;(v,w\neq0),
\]

with exactly one of the two representations using a zero.

---

### 1.  Characterisation of numbers with exactly two representations

A classical theorem on representations of an integer as a sum of two squares states that if  

\[
n = 2^{e}\,\prod_{p\equiv1\;(4)} p^{\alpha _p}\,\prod_{q\equiv3\;(4)} q^{2\beta _q},
\]

where the exponents \(\alpha _p,\beta _q\) are non‑negative integers, then the number \(r_{2}(n)\) of ordered representations \((x,y)\) (including signs and order) equals  

\[
r_{2}(n)=4\prod_{p\equiv1\;(4)}(\alpha _p+1).
\]

Thus every prime factor \(p\equiv1\;(4)\) contributes a factor \((\alpha _p+1)\) to the count, while primes \(\equiv3\;(4)\) must occur to an even power and do not affect the count.

We want \(r_{2}(n)=8\) (two unordered representations, each counted four times by signs). Therefore  

\[
4\prod_{p\equiv1\;(4)}(\alpha _p+1)=8\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\prod_{p\equiv1\;(4)}(\alpha _p+1)=2 .
\]

Consequently there is **exactly one** prime \(p\equiv1\;(4)\) dividing \(n\), and it occurs to the first power (\(\alpha _p=1\)). All other prime factors must be either \(2\) or primes \(\equiv3\;(4)\) raised to an even exponent.

Hence every admissible \(n\) has the shape  

\[
n = p\; \cdot\; 2^{e}\;\cdot\; \prod_{q\equiv3\;(4)} q^{2\beta _q},
\tag{1}
\]

where \(p\) is a prime congruent to \(1\pmod 4\), \(e\ge 0\), and the \(\beta _q\) are non‑negative integers.

---

### 2.  Ensuring that one representation contains a zero

A representation with a zero coordinate occurs precisely when \(n\) is a perfect square:

\[
n = t^{2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad (t,0),(0,t)
\]

are the four points contributed by the zero‑coordinate solution.  
Thus we must have \(n\) itself a perfect square, while still satisfying the factorisation (1).  
Writing \(n = s^{2}\) and comparing with (1) forces the exponent of the prime \(p\equiv1\;(4)\) to be **even**, i.e. \(\alpha _p = 2\). But (1) required \(\alpha _p = 1\). The only way to reconcile both conditions is to let the prime \(p\) appear **once** in the square factor and **once** outside, i.e.

\[
n = p\; \cdot\; \Bigl(p\,\cdot 2^{e}\,\prod q^{2\beta _q}\Bigr)
     = p^{2}\, 2^{e}\,\prod q^{2\beta _q}.
\]

Therefore the admissible numbers are exactly the squares of a prime \(p\equiv1\;(4)\) multiplied by a power of \(2\) and by any square of primes \(\equiv3\;(4)\). In other words  

\[
\boxed{n = p^{2}\,2^{e}\,\prod_{q\equiv3\;(4)} q^{2\beta _q}}, \qquad
p\equiv1\pmod 4,\;e\ge 0 .
\]

For each such \(n\) we have the two representations  

* \(n = (p\,\prod q^{\beta _q})^{2}+0^{2}\) (zero‑coordinate), and  
* \(n = (p\,\prod q^{\beta _q})^{2} + (2^{e/2}\!\!\prod q^{\beta _q})^{2}\) (both coordinates non‑zero),

which indeed give twelve distinct lattice points on the circle.

---

### 3.  Listing all \(n<500\)

We now enumerate all numbers of the form above with \(n<500\).

*Take \(p=5\) (the smallest prime \( \equiv1\pmod4\)).*  
\(p^{2}=25\). Multiplying by powers of \(2\) ( \(2^{0}=1,2,4,8,16\) ) we obtain  

\[
25,\; 50,\; 100,\; 200,\; 400 .
\]

Multiplying further by squares of primes \(\equiv3\pmod4\) (i.e. \(3^{2}=9,\;7^{2}=49,\;11^{2}=121,\ldots\)) quickly exceeds 500, so no additional numbers arise from \(p=5\).

*Take \(p=13\).*  
\(p^{2}=169\). Possible powers of \(2\):  

\[
169,\;338 .
\]

Both are below 500; adding any factor \(3^{2}=9\) would give \(1521>500\), so the list stops here.

*Take \(p=17\).*  
\(p^{2}=289\). Powers of \(2\) give  

\[
289,\;578\;(>500) .
\]

Thus only \(289\) is admissible.

*Take \(p=29\).*  
\(p^{2}=841>500\); no further values.

Collecting all admissible \(n\) we have  

\[
\{25,\;50,\;100,\;200,\;400,\;169,\;338,\;289\}.
\]

---

Finally we sum these eight numbers:

\[
\begin{aligned}
25+50+100+200+400 &= 775,\\

\]

\[
r_2(n)=12\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 4\prod_{p\equiv 1\;(4)}(\alpha _p+1)=12,
\]

i.e.  

\[
\prod_{p\equiv 1\;(4)}(\alpha _p+1)=3 .
\]

2. **Two distinct primes \(p_1,p_2\equiv 1\pmod 4\) each occur with exponent \(\alpha =0\).**

\[
u^{2}+v^{2}=n
\]

has **exactly 12** integer solutions \((u,v)\).  
Because \((u,v)\) and \((-u,-v)\) give the same lattice point, the 12 solutions must come in 6 opposite pairs. Consequently we need exactly **6 distinct unordered pairs** \(\{u,v\}\) with \(u^{2}+v^{2}=n\) and \(u\neq 0\) or \(v\neq 0\).

A classical result from number theory states that if  

\[
n=2^{e}\prod_{p\equiv 1\pmod 4}p^{\alpha _p}\prod_{q\equiv 3\pmod 4}q^{\beta _q},
\]

then the number \(r_2(n)\) of ordered integer solutions of \(u^{2}+v^{2}=n\) is  

\[
r_2(n)=4\prod_{p\equiv 1\pmod 4}(\alpha _p+1),
\]

provided every \(\beta _q\) is even (otherwise there are no solutions).  
The ordered count includes the four sign choices, so the number of unordered pairs is  

\[
\frac{r_2(n)}{8}= \frac{1}{2}\prod_{p\equiv 1\pmod 4}(\alpha _p+1).
\]

We require this unordered count to be \(6\). Hence  

\[
\frac{1}{2}\prod_{p\equiv 1\pmod 4}(\alpha _p+1)=6
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
\prod_{p\equiv 1\pmod 4}(\alpha _p+1)=12.
\]

Now we must factor 12 into integers each \(\ge 2\) (because \(\alpha _p\ge 1\) for a prime actually appearing). The possible factorizations are  

\[
12 = 12,\quad 12 = 6\cdot 2,\quad 12 = 4\cdot 3,\quad 12 = 3\cdot 2\cdot 2 .
\]

* a single prime \(p\equiv 1\pmod 4\) with \(\alpha _p=11\);
* two distinct primes \(p,q\equiv 1\pmod4\) with \(\alpha _p=5,\;\alpha _q=1\);
* two distinct primes \(p,q\equiv 1\pmod4\) with \(\alpha _p=3,\;\alpha _q=2\);
* three distinct primes \(p,q,r\equiv 1\pmod4\) with \(\alpha _p=2,\;\alpha _q=1,\;\alpha _r=1\).

Remember that any prime \(q\equiv 3\pmod4\) may appear only to an even exponent, and any power of \(2\) may be attached arbitrarily – they do not affect the count of representations.

We are looking for radii \(\sqrt n\) (with \(n\in \mathbb Z_{>0}\)) such that a circle whose centre is a lattice point meets **exactly** 12 lattice points.  
Because the centre is a lattice point, a lattice point \((x,y)\) lies on the circle iff  

\[
(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2=n,
\]

where \((a,b)\) is the centre and \((x-a),(y-b)\) are integers.  
Thus the number of lattice points on the circle is precisely the number of *integer solutions* \((u,v)\in\mathbb Z^2\) of

\[
u^{2}+v^{2}=n . \tag{1}
\]

Consequently the problem reduces to:

> Find all positive integers \(n<500\) for which the Diophantine equation \(u^{2}+v^{2}=n\) has exactly 12 integer solutions \((u,v)\).

(Each solution \((u,v)\) corresponds to a distinct lattice point on the circle; the centre itself is never counted because it would require \(n=0\).)

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 1. Counting representations of an integer as a sum of two squares  

For a positive integer \(n\) write its prime factorisation  

\[
n=2^{e_{0}}\prod_{p\equiv 1(4)}p^{e_{p}}\prod_{q\equiv 3(4)}q^{f_{q}} .
\]

A classical theorem of Fermat–Euler states that \(n\) can be expressed as a sum of two squares iff every prime \(q\equiv 3\pmod 4\) occurs with an **even** exponent, i.e. all \(f_{q}\) are even.  

When this condition holds, the number \(r_{2}(n)\) of *ordered* integer pairs \((u,v)\) (including signs and permutations) satisfying (1) is  

\[
r_{2}(n)=4\prod_{p\equiv 1(4)}(e_{p}+1). \tag{2}
\]

The factor \(4\) comes from the four possible sign choices \((\pm u,\pm v)\); the product accounts for the different ways to distribute prime powers among the two squares.  
If any \(f_{q}\) is odd, then \(r_{2}(n)=0\).

Because we count ordered pairs, the 12 lattice points we need correspond to  

\[
r_{2}(n)=12 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2. Solving \(4\prod_{p\equiv 1(4)}(e_{p}+1)=12\)

Dividing by 4 gives  

\[
\prod_{p\equiv 1(4)}(e_{p}+1)=3 .
\]

Since each factor \((e_{p}+1)\) is a positive integer, the only way their product equals 3 is:

* there is **exactly one** prime \(p\equiv 1\pmod4\) dividing \(n\), and for that prime \(e_{p}+1=3\), i.e. \(e_{p}=2\);
* or there are **no** such primes and the product is the empty product \(=1\), which cannot give 3.

Hence the necessary and sufficient condition is:

\[
n = 2^{e_{0}}\; p^{2}\; \prod_{q\equiv 3(4)} q^{2f_{q}}, \qquad e_{0}\ge 0,
\]

where \(p\) is a prime congruent to \(1\pmod4\) (appearing with exponent exactly 2), and every prime \(\equiv3\pmod4\) appears with an even exponent (possibly zero). The power of 2 is unrestricted because \(2\equiv2\pmod4\) does not affect the representation count.

In words: **\(n\) must contain the square of a single \(1\!\!\pmod4\) prime and may be multiplied by any square of a product of primes \(2\) or \(3\!\!\pmod4\).** No other \(1\!\!\pmod4\) prime may occur.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3. Enumerating admissible \(n<500\)

\[
5^{2}=25,\qquad 13^{2}=169,\qquad 17^{2}=289,\qquad 29^{2}=841\;(>500).
\]

**Solution**

Let the centre of the circle be the lattice point \((a,b)\) with \(a,b\in \mathbb Z\).  
The radius is \(\sqrt n\) where \(n\) is a positive integer, so the equation of the circle is  

\[
(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2=n .
\]

A lattice point \((x,y)\in\mathbb Z^2\) lies on the circle exactly when  

\[
(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2=n .
\tag{1}
\]

Thus we are looking for integer solutions \((x,y)\) of (1).  
If we translate the picture by \((-a,-b)\) we may assume without loss of generality that the centre is the origin; the number of lattice points on the circle does not change under translation. Hence we need the number of integer solutions of  

\[
x^{2}+y^{2}=n .
\tag{2}
\]

The left‑hand side is a sum of two squares. A classical result from elementary number theory says that the number of *ordered* integer solutions \((x,y)\) of (2) is  

\[
r_2(n)=4\bigl(d_1(n)-d_3(n)\bigr),
\]

where \(d_1(n)\) (resp. \(d_3(n)\)) denotes the number of positive divisors of \(n\) that are congruent to \(1\pmod 4\) (resp. \(3\pmod 4\)).  

Because the circle is symmetric, each solution \((x,y)\) with both coordinates non‑zero gives four points \((\pm x,\pm y)\); the solutions with one coordinate zero give only two points; the solution \((0,0)\) would correspond to radius \(0\) and is excluded since \(n>0\).  

Consequently, the total number of *distinct* lattice points on the circle equals  

\[
\frac{r_2(n)}{2},
\]

the factor \(2\) accounting for the fact that \((x,y)\) and \((-x,-y)\) represent the same geometric point on the circle.  

We require exactly \(12\) lattice points, so  

\[
\frac{r_2(n)}{2}=12\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad r_2(n)=24 .
\tag{3}
\]

Hence we need all positive integers \(n<500\) for which \(r_2(n)=24\).

---

### 1.  Using the divisor formula

Recall  

\[
r_2(n)=4\bigl(d_1(n)-d_3(n)\bigr).
\]

Equation (3) therefore becomes  

\[
4\bigl(d_1(n)-d_3(n)\bigr)=24\;\Longrightarrow\;d_1(n)-d_3(n)=6 .
\tag{4}
\]

Thus we must find all \(n<500\) whose divisor‑difference (1‑mod‑4 minus 3‑mod‑4) equals \(6\).

---

### 2.  Prime factorisation of numbers representable as a sum of two squares  

A positive integer can be expressed as a sum of two squares iff in its prime factorisation  

\[
n=2^{e}\,\prod_{p\equiv 1\;(4)}p^{\alpha_p}\,\prod_{q\equiv 3\;(4)}q^{2\beta_q},
\]

i.e. every prime \(q\equiv 3\pmod 4\) occurs with an **even** exponent.  

For such an \(n\) we have  

\[
d_1(n)-d_3(n)=\prod_{p\equiv 1\;(4)}(\alpha_p+1).
\tag{5}
\]

Indeed each divisor contributed by a \(p\equiv1\pmod4\) factor can be chosen independently, while the \(3\pmod4\) primes contribute equally to \(d_1\) and \(d_3\) and cancel out.

Hence condition (4) becomes  

\[
\prod_{p\equiv 1\;(4)}(\alpha_p+1)=6 .
\tag{6}
\]

The integer \(6\) factorises as \(6=6\) or \(6=3\cdot2\). Therefore the possible patterns for the exponents \(\alpha_p\) are  

* a single prime \(p\equiv 1\pmod4\) with \(\alpha_p+1=6\;\Rightarrow\;\alpha_p=5\);  

* two distinct primes \(p_1,p_2\equiv1\pmod4\) with \(\alpha_{p_1}+1=3,\;\alpha_{p_2}+1=2\), i.e. \(\alpha_{p_1}=2,\;\alpha_{p_2}=1\).

No other pattern yields product \(6\).

Thus every admissible \(n\) is of one of the two forms  

\[
\boxed{n= p^{5}\,m^2},\qquad 
\boxed{n=p^{2}\,q\,m^2},
\]

where  

* \(p,q\) are distinct primes congruent to \(1\pmod4\);  
* \(m\) is any integer (possibly \(1\)) whose prime factors are all \(\equiv 3\pmod4\) and may appear with any even exponent (including \(0\)).  
The factor \(2^{e}\) may also appear arbitrarily because it does not affect the divisor difference.

---

### 3.  Enumerating numbers below 500  

We now list all numbers \(<500\) that fit the two patterns.

#### (a)  Numbers of the form \(p^{5}m^{2}\)

The smallest prime \(p\equiv1\pmod4\) is \(5\).  

\[
5^{5}=3125>500,
\]

so no number of this type lies below \(500\). Hence this case contributes nothing.

#### (b) Numbers of the form \(p^{2}q\,m^{2}\)

Take distinct \(p,q\equiv1\pmod4\). The smallest such primes are \(5\) and \(13\); the next are \(5, 17\); \(13,17\); etc.  

We also may multiply by a square of a product of \(3\pmod4\) primes (including the empty product, i.e. \(m=1\)).  

Because we must stay below \(500\), we first list the basic products \(p^{2}q\) (with \(m=1\)).  

| \(p\) | \(q\) | \(p^{2}q\) |
|------|------|-----------|
| 5    | 13   | \(5^{2}\cdot13 = 325\) |
| 5    | 17   | \(5^{2}\cdot17 = 425\) |

Each solution \((u,v)\) gives a lattice point on the circle, and conversely every lattice point on the circle corresponds to a unique solution \((u,v)\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Counting solutions of \(u^{2}+v^{2}=n\)

If \((u,v)\) is a solution, then so are \((\pm u,\pm v)\) and \((\pm v,\pm u)\).  
Hence the total number of integer solutions is a multiple of 8, except when a coordinate is zero (which yields only 4 symmetric points) or when \(|u|=|v|\) (which yields only 4 points as well).  

For a given \(n\) let  

\[
r_2(n)=\#\{(u,v)\in\mathbb Z^{2}\mid u^{2}+v^{2}=n\}.
\]

A classical result from elementary number theory states  

\[
r_2(n)=4\bigl(d_1(n)-d_3(n)\bigr),
\]

where \(d_1(n)\) (resp. \(d_3(n)\)) denotes the number of positive divisors of \(n\) that are congruent to \(1\) (resp. \(3\)) modulo 4.  
In particular, \(r_2(n)\) is always a multiple of 4.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  When is \(r_2(n)=12\)?

We need \(r_2(n)=12\). From the formula above this means  

\[
4\bigl(d_1(n)-d_3(n)\bigr)=12\quad\Longrightarrow\quad d_1(n)-d_3(n)=3.
\]

Thus we must find all \(n<500\) for which the difference between the numbers of \(1\pmod4\) and \(3\pmod4\) divisors equals 3.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Structure of such \(n\)

Write the prime factorisation of \(n\) as  

\[
n=2^{e}\prod_{p\equiv1(4)}p^{\alpha_p}\prod_{q\equiv3(4)}q^{\beta_q},
\]

where the products run over distinct odd primes of the indicated residue class.
A divisor of \(n\) is congruent to \(1\pmod4\) precisely when it contains an even total exponent of the primes \(q\equiv3(4)\); otherwise it is \(3\pmod4\).

Consequently  

\[
d_1(n)-d_3(n)=\Bigl(\prod_{p\equiv1(4)}(\alpha_p+1)\Bigr)
               \Bigl(\prod_{q\equiv3(4)}(\beta_q+1)\Bigr)_{\! \text{even exponent sum}}
               \;-\;
               \Bigl(\prod_{p\equiv1(4)}(\alpha_p+1)\Bigr)
               \Bigl(\prod_{q\equiv3(4)}(\beta_q+1)\Bigr)_{\! \text{odd exponent sum}} .
\]

The factor contributed by the prime 2 is irrelevant because \(2\equiv2\pmod4\) and never changes the residue class of a divisor.

The expression above simplifies dramatically: the two products differ only by a sign, so  

\[
d_1(n)-d_3(n)=\Bigl(\prod_{p\equiv1(4)}(\alpha_p+1)\Bigr)
               \Bigl(\prod_{q\equiv3(4)}(\beta_q+1)\Bigr)\, \times
               \begin{cases}
               1 &\text{if the total exponent of the }q\text{'s is even},\\[2pt]
               -1&\text{if it is odd}.
               \end{cases}
\]

Hence the absolute value \(|d_1(n)-d_3(n)|\) equals the product of \((\alpha_p+1)\) over the \(1\pmod4\) primes times the product of \((\beta_q+1)\) over the \(3\pmod4\) primes.

n = p^{2}\quad\text{with }p\equiv1\pmod4,
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
n = q^{2}\quad\text{with }q\equiv3\pmod4,
\]

Let the centre of the circle be the lattice point \((a,b)\) and let the radius be \(\sqrt{n}\) with \(n\in \mathbb Z_{>0}\).
A lattice point \((x,y)\) lies on the circle exactly when  

\[
(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2=n .
\]

Because the centre \((a,b)\) has integer coordinates, the change of variables  

\[
u=x-a,\qquad v=y-b
\]

converts the equation to  

\[
u^{2}+v^{2}=n ,\qquad u,v\in\mathbb Z .
\]

Hence the number of lattice points on the circle is exactly the number of integer
solutions \((u,v)\) of \(u^{2}+v^{2}=n\).  
Denote this number by \(r_{2}(n)\).  
We are asked for those \(n<500\) for which \(r_{2}(n)=12\).

---

### 1.  The formula for \(r_{2}(n)\)

Write the prime factorisation of \(n\) as  

\[
n=2^{\alpha}\!\!\!\prod_{p\equiv 1\;(4)} p^{\beta _p}
      \!\!\!\prod_{q\equiv 3\;(4)} q^{2\gamma _q},
\]

that is, every prime \(q\equiv 3\pmod 4\) occurs with an **even** exponent
(otherwise \(n\) would not be a sum of two squares).  
With this notation the classical theorem on representations of an integer as a
sum of two squares gives  

\[
r_{2}(n)=4\!\!\prod_{p\equiv 1\;(4)} (\beta _p+1).
\tag{1}
\]

Only the primes \(p\equiv 1\pmod 4\) influence the value of \(r_{2}(n)\).

---

### 2.  Imposing \(r_{2}(n)=12\)

Equation (1) shows that \(r_{2}(n)\) is a multiple of \(4\).  
Thus \(r_{2}(n)=12\) is equivalent to  

\[
\prod_{p\equiv 1\;(4)} (\beta _p+1)=3 .
\tag{2}
\]

The integer factor‑product on the left can be \(3\) only in one way:
there is **exactly one** prime \(p\equiv 1\pmod 4\) occurring in the factorisation
of \(n\) and its exponent \(\beta _p\) must be \(2\) (because \(2+1=3\)).
All other primes \(\equiv 1\pmod 4\) are absent, while any prime
\(\equiv 3\pmod 4\) may appear, but only with an even exponent.

Consequently every admissible \(n\) has the shape  

\[
n = 2^{\alpha}\,p^{2}\,s^{2},
\tag{3}
\]

where  

* \(p\) is a prime with \(p\equiv 1\pmod 4\);
* \(\alpha\ge 0\) is an integer;
* \(s\) is any integer whose prime factors are all \(\equiv 3\pmod 4\)
  (the square guarantees the required even exponents).

Conversely, any integer of the form (3) indeed satisfies \(r_{2}(n)=12\).

---

### 3.  Enumerating the possibilities with \(n<500\)

\[
